claims.evidence: The domain architecture is described in the text and supported by protein disorder prediction data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: MSIL1-4 genes are widely expressed in Arabidopsis, with MSIL1 showing the lowest levels of expression.
claims.source: The survey of the gene expression ARAPORT11 databases (https://araport.org/; http://fgcz-pep2pro.uzh.ch) revealed that the MSIL1-4 genes are widely expressed in Arabidopsis, with MSIL1 showing the lowest levels of expression (Figure 1C).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq expression data from ARAPORT11 database shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: MSIL orthologs are widely distributed in land plants, from bryophytes to angiosperms.
claims.source: Database searches further indicated that MSIL orthologs are widely distributed in land plants, from bryophytes to angiosperms (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by conservation tracks from MUSCLE software showing MSIL orthologs across multiple plant species presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: MSIL2 and MSIL4 proteins show a diffuse cytoplasmic distribution in root cells of stable Arabidopsis transgenic plants.
claims.source: Both proteins showed a diffuse cytoplasmic distribution in root cells of stable Arabidopsis transgenic plants that contrasts with the nucleus and cytoplasmic distributions of the free GFP protein control (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: The subcellular localization is determined by fluorescence microscopy on GFP-tagged versions of MSIL2 and MSIL4 shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: The msil2-1/msil4-1 (msil2/4) double mutant shows developmental abnormal phenotypes, including enlarged and curled leaves, early leaf senescence and a pendant inflorescence stem.
claims.source: Only the msil2-1/msil4-1 (msil2/4) double mutant showed discernable developmental abnormal phenotypes, including enlarged and curled leaves, early leaf senescence and a pendant inflorescence stem (Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
claims.evidence: The phenotypes are documented through photographs and observations of the msil2/4 double mutant compared to wild-type plants shown in Figures 1E, 1F, and supplementary figures.

claims.claim: The msil1-1/msil2-1/msil3-1/msil4-1 (msil1/2/3/4) quadruple mutant shows no particular or aggravated developmental phenotypes with respect to the msil2/4 double mutant.
claims.source: To assess whether MSIL1 and MSIL3 also contribute to Arabidopsis development in the msil2/4 double mutant background, we generated a msil1-1/msil2-1/msil3-1/msil4-1 (msil1/2/3/4) quadruple mutant that shows no particular or aggravated developmental phenotypes with respect to the msil2/4 double mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C).
claims.evidence: The phenotypic comparison is documented in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A–C showing similar phenotypes between msil2/4 and msil1/2/3/4 mutants.

claims.claim: Ectopic expression of either MSIL2F or MSIL4F proteins rescues all the phenotypes associated with the MSIL2/4 defect.
claims.source: The ectopic expression of either MSIL2F or MSIL4F proteins was able to rescue all the phenotypes associated with the MSIL2/4 defect (Figure 1E and F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3E).
claims.evidence: The complementation is demonstrated by phenotypic rescue in transgenic plants expressing Flag/HA-tagged versions of MSIL2 or MSIL4 shown in Figures 1E, 1F, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3E.

claims.claim: MSIL2 and MSIL4 redundantly control various aspects of development in Arabidopsis.
claims.source: This confirms that MSIL2F and MSIL4F are functional proteins and more importantly that MSIL2 and MSIL4 redundantly control various aspects of development in Arabidopsis.
claims.evidence: The functional redundancy is inferred from the complementation experiments showing that either MSIL2 or MSIL4 can rescue the msil2/4 mutant phenotypes.

claims.claim: MSILs are very similar to metazoan MSIs over their RRM sequences.
claims.source: MSILs are very similar to metazoan MSIs over their RRM sequences (Figure 1A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
claims.evidence: The sequence similarity is shown through amino acid identity percentages in Figure 1A and multiple sequence alignment in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Homology models of the MSIL4 RRM motifs generated using SWISS-MODEL and AlphaFold2 servers show structural similarity to metazoan MSI RRM domains.
claims.source: a closeness of sequences also observed when homology models of the MSIL4 RRM motifs were generated using SWISS-MODEL (Biasini et al., 2014) and AlphaFold2 (Jumper et al., 2021) servers (Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: The structural similarity is demonstrated through homology modeling shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: MSIL RRM domains adopt the characteristic RRM fold with a four-stranded β-sheet structure bearing conserved phenylalanine residues involved in specific recognition of RNA bases.
claims.source: Homology-based structure prediction proposed that these domains adopt the characteristic RRM fold with a four-stranded β-sheet structure bearing the conserved phenylalanine residues involved in the specific recognition of RNA bases (Daubner et al., 2013; Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The structural features are predicted through homology modeling and supported by citation to established RRM structure knowledge (Daubner et al., 2013), shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: MSIL2/4 proteins are identified in the experimentally determined Arabidopsis mRNA-binding proteome.
claims.source: This supports the idea that MSILs have retained the ability to interact with RNA, a notion further supported by the identification of MSIL2/4 proteins in the experimentally determined Arabidopsis mRNA-binding proteome (Reichel et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published proteomics study (Reichel et al., 2016) that identified MSIL2/4 as mRNA-binding proteins.

claims.claim: MSIL4, but not MSIL4RRM (RNA-binding mutant), exhibits intrinsic RNA binding activity in vitro.
claims.source: Protein-RNA interaction assays using RNA homopolymers immobilized on agarose beads confirmed that the MSIL4, but not MSIL4RRM, exhibited intrinsic RNA binding activity in vitro (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: The RNA-binding activity is demonstrated through in vitro binding assays with RNA homopolymers shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: MSIL4G, but not MSIL4GRRM proteins, can rescue the developmental defects incurred by MSIL2/4 mutations.
claims.source: MSIL4G, but not MSIL4GRRM proteins were able to rescue the developmental defects incurred by MSIL2/4 mutations (Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C)
claims.evidence: The complementation results are shown through phenotypic analysis in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–C.

claims.claim: RRM-dependent RNA-binding activity is essential for MSIL2/4 functions in vivo.
claims.source: indicating that these proteins are likely to exert their functions by interacting with RNA targets in vivo.
claims.evidence: The requirement for RNA-binding is inferred from the failure of RRM mutant proteins to complement the msil2/4 phenotype.

claims.claim: MSIL2F1 and MSIL4F1 exhibit a similar protein interaction network, with 27 proteins significantly enriched in both MS analyses.
claims.source: Consistent with their functional redundancy, MSIL2F1 and MSIL4F1 exhibit a similar protein interaction network, with 27 proteins significantly enriched in both MS analyses (Figure 3A and B, and Supplementary file 1).
claims.evidence: The protein interaction networks are determined through affinity purification coupled to LC-MS/MS analysis shown in Figure 3A and B.

claims.claim: MSIL2F1/4F1 protein-protein interaction network is principally enriched in poly(A) binding protein, mRNA 3-UTR binding, single-stranded RNA binding, and translation initiation factor activity GO molecular functions.
claims.source: Examination of the PANTHER database (http://www.pantherdb.org) identified that MSIL2F1/4F1 are part of a protein-protein interaction network that was principally enriched in 4 categories of GO molecular functions, namely poly(A) binding protein (GO:0008143), mRNA 3-UTR binding (GO:0003730), single-stranded RNA binding (GO:0003727), and translation initiation factor activity (GO:0003743), highlighting the relationship between MSIL2/4 and the mRNA binding and regulatory proteome (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: The GO enrichment analysis is performed on the MSIL2/4 interactome data and shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: MSIL2G/4G, like PAB2R, show a dispersed cytoplasmic signal under normal condition, and are recruited to cytoplasmic granules that largely overlap with PAB2R-containing stress granules upon heat stress.
claims.source: Fluorescence analysis revealed that MSIL2G/4 G, like PAB2R, show a dispersed cytoplasmic signal under normal condition, and are recruited to cytoplasmic granules that largely overlap with PAB2R-containing SG upon heat stress as judged by the yellow-orange appearance in the merged figure (Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
claims.evidence: The colocalization is demonstrated through fluorescence microscopy showing MSIL2G/4G and PAB2R localization before and after heat stress in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Treatment with cycloheximide (CHX), a translation inhibitor, prevents the formation of MSIL2G/4G and PAB2R cytoplasmic foci, confirming that those foci correspond to bona fide stress granules.
claims.source: Treatment with cycloheximide (CHX), a translation inhibitor that prevent SG assembly by trapping mRNAs at polysomes (Mahboubi and Stochaj, 2017), confirmed that those foci correspond to bonafide SGs (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: The stress granule identity is confirmed through CHX treatment experiments shown in Figure 3E, supported by citation to established knowledge about CHX effects (Mahboubi and Stochaj, 2017).

claims.claim: MSIL2/4 genes are highly expressed in the SCW-forming interfascicular fiber (if) and xylem vessel (xy) cells of Arabidopsis inflorescence stem.
claims.source: Survey of the Arabidopsis inflorescence stem tissue-specific transcriptome database (Shi et al., 2021) indicated that the MSIL2/4 genes are highly expressed in the SCW-forming interfascicular fiber (if) and xylem vessel (xy) cells (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: The tissue-specific expression is shown through transcriptome database analysis (Shi et al., 2021) presented in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The interfascicular fiber cells display a significantly thinner SCW in msil2/4 mutant compared to wild-type.
claims.source: However, the examination of the cell wall thickness in cross sections of stems revealed that the interfascicular fiber cells display a significantly thinner SCW in msil2/4 mutant (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: The cell wall thickness is measured in stem cross-sections and quantified in Figure 4C showing significant reduction in msil2/4 mutant.

claims.claim: UV autofluorescence and phloroglucinol staining reveal a reduced lignin signal in the interfascicular fibers of the msil2/4 mutant compared to Col-0 or complemented plants.
claims.source: UV autofluorescence and phloroglucinol staining of the Col-0, msil2/4, msil2/4+MSIL2 F1, and msil2/4+MSIL4 F1 stem sections revealed a reduced lignin signal in the interfascicular fibers of the msil2/4 mutant compared to Col-0 or complemented plants (Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The lignin content is assessed through UV autofluorescence and phloroglucinol staining shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: A significant decrease of 30% in AcBr lignin content was observed in the msil2/4 mutant compared to the Col-0 control plants.
claims.source: In agreement with these observations, a significant decrease of 30% in AcBr lignin content was observed in the msil2/4 mutant compared to the Col-0 control plants (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: The lignin content is quantified using acetyl bromide (AcBr) method and shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: Total monomer yield from thioacidolysis did not significantly differ between the Col-0 and the msil2/4 mutant.
claims.source: Total monomer yield did not significantly differ between the Col-0 and the msil2/4 mutant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that the structure of the lignin polymer is not significantly affected in the mutant.
claims.evidence: The lignin composition is analyzed through thioacidolysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Calcofluor white staining reveals an increased signal in the interfascicular fiber cells of msil2/4 mutant, supporting changes in the composition/accessibility of cellulose.
claims.source: Further examination of β-glucan composition using the fluorescent dye calcofluor white (Herth and Schnepf, 1980) revealed an increased staining in the interfascicular fiber cells of msil2/4 mutant, supporting changes in the composition/accessibility of cellulose (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: The cellulose composition/accessibility is assessed through calcofluor white staining shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, with citation to the method (Herth and Schnepf, 1980).

claims.claim: A higher amount of reducing sugars from native cell wall (without pre-treatment) was released using msil2/4 samples compared to Col-0 samples.
claims.source: A higher amount of reducing sugars from native cell wall (without pre-treatment/-Tr) was released using msil2/4 samples compared to Col-0 samples.
claims.evidence: The saccharification yield is measured and compared between Col-0 and msil2/4 samples.

claims.claim: After cell wall loosening using alkali pre-treatment, an even more important amount of sugars (+5%) was released from double mutants CW enzymatic digestion.
claims.source: After cell wall loosening using alkali pre-treatment/+, an even more important amounts of sugars (+5%) was released from double mutants CW enzymatic digestion (Figure 4G).
claims.evidence: The saccharification yield after alkali pre-treatment is measured and shown in Figure 4G.

claims.claim: MSIL2/4 regulate the molecular architecture of SCW in the interfascicular fibers, contributing significantly to the setting of biomass recalcitrance in Arabidopsis.
claims.source: Together, our data indicate that MSIL2/4 regulate the molecular architecture of SCW in the interfascicular fibers, contributing significantly to the setting of biomass recalcitrance in Arabidopsis.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from multiple lines of evidence including cell wall thickness, lignin content, cellulose accessibility, and saccharification yield measurements.

claims.claim: 234 genes were found to be significantly differentially regulated (DEG) in the msil2/4 mutant background, including 156 up-regulated and 78 down-regulated mRNAs.
claims.source: In total, we found 234 genes to be significantly differentially regulated (DEG) in the msil2/4 mutant background (with stringent thresholds having a logarithm of fold change >1.5 or<−1.5 and false discovery rate FDR ≤0.05), including 156 up-regulated and 78 down-regulated mRNAs (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A, and Supplementary file 3).
claims.evidence: The differentially expressed genes are identified through mRNA sequencing analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and Supplementary file 3.

claims.claim: Genes encoding regulatory or enzymatic components of the SCW biosynthesis pathway were absent from the DEG list, and their expression was not significantly changed in msil2/4 mutant.
claims.source: Interestingly, genes encoding regulatory or enzymatic components of the SCW biosynthesis pathway were absent from the DEG list, and their expression was not significant changed in msil2/4 mutant (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The expression levels of SCW biosynthesis genes are analyzed in the RNA-seq data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Gene Ontology analysis of DEGs revealed significantly enriched signaling pathways (FDR ≤0.05) involved in plant defense or responses to biotic and abiotic stresses.
claims.source: Gene Ontology analysis of DEGs revealed significantly enriched signaling pathways (FDR ≤0.05) involved in plant defense or responses to biotic and abiotic stresses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
claims.evidence: The GO enrichment analysis is performed on the DEGs and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Comparative proteomic analysis revealed 267 proteins with significant abundances in the msil2/4 mutant versus Col-0 inflorescence stems (fold change ≥2, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR <1%), including 156 up-regulated, and 111 down-regulated proteins.
claims.source: This analysis revealed 267 proteins with significant abundances in the msil2/4 mutant versus Col-0 inflorescence stems (fold change ≥2, Benjamini-Hochberg FDR <1%), including 156 up-regulated, and 111 down-regulated proteins (Figure 5A and Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The differentially abundant proteins are identified through MS-based quantitative proteomics shown in Figure 5A and Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: The up-regulated proteins in msil2/4 mutant show strong enrichment in enzymes involved in the glucuronoxylan biosynthetic pathway.
claims.source: While no specific GO terms were enriched in the set of down-regulated proteins, the inspection of the up-regulated proteins revealed a strong enrichment in enzymes involved in the glucuronoxylan biosynthetic pathway (Figure 5A and B, and Supplementary file 4).
claims.evidence: The GO enrichment analysis of up-regulated proteins is shown in Figure 5A and B, and Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: The upregulated glucuronoxylan-related proteins included glycosyltransferases required for the xylan backbone synthesis (IRX9/10/14), as well as enzymes involved in its substitution (ESK1, GUX1, and GXM3).
claims.source: Notably, the upregulated glucuronoxylan-related proteins included glycosyltransferases required for the xylan backbone synthesis (IRX9/10/14), as well as enzymes involved in its substitution (ESK1, GUX1, and GXM3) (Scheller and Ulvskov, 2010; Figure 5A–C).
claims.evidence: The specific upregulated proteins are identified in the proteomic analysis shown in Figure 5A–C, with citation to their known functions (Scheller and Ulvskov, 2010).

claims.claim: The observed proteomic changes in msil2/4 were not associated with significant variations in mRNA levels of the up-regulated glucuronoxylan-related genes.
claims.source: Visual inspection of the RNA-seq aligned reads of the up-regulated glucuronoxylan-related genes using the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) and quantitative RT-PCR analysis of the glucuronoxylan-related decoration genes confirmed that the observed proteomic changes in msil2/4 were not associated with significant variations in mRNA levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B).
claims.evidence: The mRNA levels are analyzed through RNA-seq and qRT-PCR shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B.

claims.claim: The levels of glucose (Glc) and xylose (Xyl), which are the building blocks of cellulose and xylan polysaccharides in the SCW, were not substantially affected in the msil2/4 mutant.
claims.source: The levels of glucose (Glc) and xylose (Xyl), which are the building blocks of cellulose and xylan polysaccharides in the SCW were not substantially affected in the msil2/4 mutant (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: The monosaccharide composition is analyzed and shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: No major changes were observed in the levels of the primary cell wall-related monosaccharides (galactose, rhamnose, arabinose, mannose, fucose) in the msil2/4 mutant.
claims.source: Similarly, no major changes were observed in the levels of the primary cell wall-related monosaccharides, galactose, rhamnose, arabinose, mannose, fucose (Figure 5D)
claims.evidence: The monosaccharide composition is analyzed and shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: LM11 antibody shows a similar signal in the interfascicular and xylary fibers of Col-0 and msil2/4 mutant stems, confirming that the glucuronoxylan content was not significantly modified in msil2/4 compared to Col-0.
claims.source: LM11, which binds with similar affinity both unsubstituted and substituted glucuronoxylan, shows a similar signal in the interfascicular and xylary fibers of Col-0 and msil2/4 mutant stems, confirming that the glucuronoxylan content was not significantly modified in msil2/4 compared to Col-0 (Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: The glucuronoxylan content is assessed through immunofluorescence labeling with LM11 antibody shown in Figure 5E.

claims.claim: LM10 antibody shows a significant signal decrease in the interfascicular fibers of msil2/4 mutant compared to Col-0.
claims.source: In contrast, LM10, which binds less efficiently the substituted glucuronoxylan (McCartney et al., 2006), shows a significant signal decrease in the interfascicular fibers of msil2/4 mutant (Figure 5E and Supplementary file 5).
claims.evidence: The glucuronoxylan decoration is assessed through immunofluorescence labeling with LM10 antibody shown in Figure 5E and Supplementary file 5, with citation to the antibody specificity (McCartney et al., 2006).

claims.claim: The MSIL2/4 mutations impact the accumulation and activity of the glucuronoxylan decoration machinery in the interfascicular fiber cells of Arabidopsis stem.
claims.source: Together, our data indicate that the MSIL2/4 mutations impact the accumulation and activity of the glucuronoxylan decoration machinery in the interfascicular fiber cells of Arabidopsis stem.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the proteomic data showing overaccumulation of glucuronoxylan biosynthetic enzymes and the immunofluorescence data showing changes in glucuronoxylan decoration.

claims.claim: MALDI-TOF analysis of Col-0 glucuronoxylan oligosaccharides showed the release of xylo-oligosaccharide pairs, evenly spaced by their degrees of polymerization and acetylation, bearing a GlcA or methylated GlcA substitution group.
claims.source: Consistent with previous observations (Mortimer et al., 2010; Urbanowicz et al., 2012), MALDI-TOF analysis of Col-0 glucurononoxylan oligosaccharides showed the release of xylo-oligosaccharide pairs, evenly spaced by their degrees of polymerization and acetylation, bearing a GlcA (m/z 1705.5/1747.5) or methylated GlcA (m/z 1719.5/1761.5) substitution group (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The xylo-oligosaccharide patterns are analyzed through MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry shown in Figure 6A, with citations to previous observations (Mortimer et al., 2010; Urbanowicz et al., 2012).

claims.claim: The level of GlcA branched xylo-oligomers was strongly decreased in the msil2/4 double mutant.
claims.source: Interestingly, the level of GlcA branched xylo-oligomers was strongly decreased in the msil2/4 double mutant, and this whatever the complexity of the oligomers considered (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: The xylo-oligosaccharide patterns are analyzed through MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The molecular phenotypes observed in the msil2/4 mutant were rescued in both msil2/4+MSIL2 F1 and msil2/4+MSIL4 F1 complemented lines.
claims.source: Importantly, the molecular phenotypes observed in the msil2/4 mutant were rescued in both msil2/4+MSIL2 F1 and msil2/4+MSIL4 F1 complemented lines, confirming the specificity of the mutation (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: The rescue of molecular phenotypes is shown through MALDI-TOF analysis of complemented lines in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Quantification of the acidic sugar levels confirmed that the release of GlcA moiety was strongly reduced in msil2/4 double mutant, as opposed to the galacturonic acid/GalA group located on pectins.
claims.source: In agreement with the MALDI–TOF outcome, quantification of the acidic sugar levels in unpretreated (-), or acid pretreated (+) WT and msil2/4 stem samples confirmed that the release of GlcA moiety was strongly reduced in msil2/4 double mutant, as opposed to the galacturonic acid/GalA group located on pectins (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: The acidic monosaccharide composition is analyzed and shown in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: Upon normalization with spike-in control, the MALDI-TOF data indicated that the decrease of the peaks corresponding to the GlcA-branched xylooligosaccharides was correlated with an increase in corresponding meGlcA branched xylooligosaccharides.
claims.source: Upon normalization, the MALDI-TOF data indicated that the decrease of the peaks corresponding to the GlcA-branched xylooligosaccharides was correlated with a increase in corresponding meGlcA branched xylooligosaccharides, (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 6)
claims.evidence: The normalized MALDI-TOF data with spike-in control is shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, Supplementary file 6.

claims.claim: The MSIL2/4 mutations unleash the activity of the GXM1/3 in stem.
claims.source: suggesting that the MSIL2/4 mutations unleash the activity of the GXM1/3 in stem.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the MALDI-TOF data showing increased methylation of glucuronoxylan in msil2/4 mutant.

claims.claim: GXM3 and GXM1 mRNAs are efficiently pulled-down from MSIL4G-3, but not MSIL4GRRM-3 plant extracts.
claims.source: RNA immunoprecipitation assays further confirmed that the GXM3 and GXM1 mRNAs are efficiently pulled-down from MSIL4G-3, but not MSIL4GRRM-3 plant extracts (Figure 6D)
claims.evidence: The RNA-protein interaction is demonstrated through RNA immunoprecipitation assays shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: The MSIL2/4 interaction network controls the 4-O-methylation of glucuronoxylan by repressing the activity of the GXM1/3 mRNAs in stem.
claims.source: suggesting that the MSIL2/4 interaction network controls the 4-O-methylation of glucuronoxylan by repressing the activity of the GXM1/3 mRNAs in stem.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the RNA immunoprecipitation data showing MSIL4 binds GXM mRNAs and the increased glucuronoxylan methylation in msil2/4 mutant.

claims.claim: MSIL2 and MSIL4 function redundantly to control various aspects of Arabidopsis development, including leaf senescence, morphology of rosette leaves, and the rigidity of the inflorescence stem.
claims.source: We found that two of the four MSIL members, MSIL2 and MSIL4, function redundantly to control various aspects of Arabidopsis development, including leaf senescence, morphology of rosette leaves, and the rigidity of the inflorescence stem.
claims.evidence: The functional redundancy is demonstrated through the phenotypic analysis of single and double mutants.

claims.claim: The pleiotropy associated with the MSIL2/4 mutation likely results from the multifunctionality of these proteins in Arabidopsis development.
claims.source: Our data suggest that the pleiotropy associated with the MSIL2/4 mutation likely results from the multifunctionality of these proteins in Arabidopsis development, a situation similar to the complex phenotypic traits previously associated to MSI mutations in animals (Fox et al., 2015; Kudinov et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: The interpretation is based on the multiple phenotypes observed in msil2/4 mutant and comparison to animal MSI functions, supported by citations (Fox et al., 2015; Kudinov et al., 2017; Nguyen et al., 2020).

claims.claim: The animal polyA-binding protein/PABP (homolog of the plant PABs) was previously shown to be a functional partner of MSI that is essential for its activity in translation repression.
claims.source: Notably, the animal polyA-binding protein/PABP (homolog of the plant PABs) was previously shown to be a functional partner of MSI that is essential for it activity in translation repression (Fox et al., 2015; Cragle et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Fox et al., 2015; Cragle et al., 2019) showing PABP as a functional partner of MSI.

claims.claim: The rbgd2/4 double mutant exhibits no developmental phenotypes under normal growth conditions.
claims.source: In accordance with this observation, the MSILs and RBGDs clearly diversify in function, since the rbgd2/4 double mutant exhibits no developmental phenotypes under normal growth conditions.
claims.evidence: The phenotypic observation of rbgd2/4 mutant is stated in the text.

claims.claim: MSIL2 and MSIL4 function redundantly to promote SCW formation in the interfascicular fibers and their ability to bind RNA is essential to fulfill this function.
claims.source: In this study, we show that MSIL2 and MSIL4, function redundantly to promote SCW formation in the interfascicular fibers and that their ability to bind RNA is essential to fulfill this function.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is based on the complementation experiments showing that RRM mutant proteins cannot rescue the msil2/4 phenotype.

claims.claim: The fiber-specific effect of the MSIL2/4 mutations on SCW formation is supported by evidence showing that the msil2/4 mutant grows normally and lacks the xylem collapses usually observed in more pleiotropic SCW deficient mutants.
claims.source: The fiber-specific effect of the MSIL2/4 mutations on SCW formation, is further supported by our evidence showing that the msil2/4 mutant grows normally and lacks the xylem collapses usually observed in more pleiotropic SCW deficient mutants.
claims.evidence: The observation is based on microscopic analysis of stem cross-sections showing no xylem collapse in msil2/4 mutant.

claims.claim: Specific master transcriptional regulators, such as NST1 and NST3, control cell-lineage-specific formation of SCW formation in Arabidopsis.
claims.source: Previous studies have shown that specific master transcriptional regulators, such as NST1 and NST3, control cell-lineage-specific formation of SCW formation in Arabidopsis (Taylor-Teeples et al., 2015; Mitsuda et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Taylor-Teeples et al., 2015; Mitsuda et al., 2007) showing NST1 and NST3 control cell-lineage-specific SCW formation.

claims.claim: RBP-mediated post-transcriptional mechanisms are involved in cell-type-specific control of SCW formation in Arabidopsis.
claims.source: Our study extends this observation by showing that RBP-mediated post-transcriptional mechanisms are also involved in cell-type-specific control of SCW formation in Arabidopsis.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is based on the fiber-specific effects of MSIL2/4 mutations on SCW formation.

claims.claim: The presumed role of MSIL2/4 in SCW formation in the interfascicular fiber cells contrasts with the rather constitutive expression of the corresponding MSIL2/4 genes.
claims.source: Notably, the presumed role of MSIL2/4 in SCW formation in the interfascicular fiber cells contrasts with the rather constitutive expression of the corresponding MSIL2/4 genes, suggesting as previously discussed, that MSIL2/4 activities depend on cell-context.
claims.evidence: The observation is based on the comparison between the constitutive expression pattern of MSIL2/4 genes and their fiber-specific function.

claims.claim: The ubiquitous MSI2 in animals shows cell-type specific activities in cell renewal, cell differentiation and cancer control.
claims.source: This is in accordance with the reported cell-type specific activities of the ubiquitous MSI2 in cell renewal, cell differentiation and cancer control in animals (Fox et al., 2015; Kudinov et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Fox et al., 2015; Kudinov et al., 2017) showing cell-type specific activities of MSI2 in animals.

claims.claim: The constitutive activation of defense pathways has been well documented in mutant plants defective in cell wall formation, including the SCW.
claims.source: In this regard, the constitutive activation of defense pathways has been well documented in mutant plants defective in cell wall formation, including the SCW (Ellis et al., 2002; Miedes et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2023)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Ellis et al., 2002; Miedes et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2023) documenting defense pathway activation in cell wall mutants.

claims.claim: The accumulation of the mRNA of SCW biosynthesis enzymes and regulators are unaffected in the msil2/4 mutant.
claims.source: Our data reveal that the accumulation of the mRNA of SCW biosynthesis enzymes and regulators are unaffected in the msil2/4 mutant, suggesting that the MSIL2/4 proteins act at a translational level to regulate the SCW formation.
claims.evidence: The mRNA levels are analyzed through RNA-seq and qRT-PCR showing no significant changes in SCW biosynthesis genes.

claims.claim: MSIL2/4 proteins act at a translational level to regulate the SCW formation.
claims.source: Our data reveal that the accumulation of the mRNA of SCW biosynthesis enzymes and regulators are unaffected in the msil2/4 mutant, suggesting that the MSIL2/4 proteins act at a translational level to regulate the SCW formation.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that mRNA levels are unchanged while protein levels are altered in msil2/4 mutant.

claims.claim: Proteins related to the glucuronoxylan biosynthesis machinery, including enzymes involved both in the synthesis (IRX9/10/14) and substitution (GUX1, ESK1, and GXM3) of the xylan backbone, are significantly over-accumulated in the msil2/4 mutant.
claims.source: Indeed, our MS data reveal that proteins related to the glucuronoxylan biosynthesis machinery, including enzymes involved both in the synthesis (IRX9/10/14) and substitution (GUX1, ESK1, and GXM3) of the xylan backbone, are significantly over-accumulated in the msil2/4 mutant.
claims.evidence: The protein overaccumulation is identified through MS-based quantitative proteomics.

claims.claim: MSIL2/4 is exerting a multilevel control on the glucuronoxylan pathway.
claims.source: Knowing that the synthesis of the structurally complex glucuronoxylan polysaccharide requires the coordinated production and action of these enzymes in the Golgi apparatus, our results suggests that MSIL2/4 is exerting a multilevel control on the glucuronoxylan pathway, a mechanism reminiscent of the multi-nodal control displays by MSI2 on the TGF-β and translation pathways in animal cells (Park et al., 2014; Duggimpudi et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the overaccumulation of multiple glucuronoxylan biosynthetic enzymes in msil2/4 mutant, with comparison to MSI2 function in animals supported by citations (Park et al., 2014; Duggimpudi et al., 2018).

claims.claim: The steady-state levels of glucuronoxylan and cellulose are correlated within the SCW.
claims.source: Alternatively, in light with prior studies that have shown that the steady-state levels of glucuronoxylan and cellulose are correlated within the SCW (Wu et al., 2009; Ye and Zhong, 2022)
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Wu et al., 2009; Ye and Zhong, 2022) showing correlation between glucuronoxylan and cellulose levels.

claims.claim: GXM-mediated methylation is a rate-limiting step in glucuronoxylan that can be overcome by GXM protein overexpression.
claims.source: In contrast, the concomitance between the glucuronoxylan hypermethylation and the GXM3 overaccumulation phenotypes observed in msil2/4 clearly support the previous assumption that GXM-mediated methylation is a rate-limiting step in glucuronoxylan that can be overcome by GXM protein overexpression (Yuan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The conclusion is based on the correlation between GXM3 overaccumulation and increased glucuronoxylan methylation in msil2/4 mutant, supported by citation to previous work (Yuan et al., 2014).

claims.claim: Transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation act in a concerted manner to fine tune the GXM3 and glucuronoxylan methylation levels in the stem.
claims.source: In fine, our data support the idea that transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation act in a concerted manner to fine tune the GXM3 and glucuronoxylan methylation levels in the stem.
claims.evidence: The conclusion is inferred from the observation that both transcriptional and post-transcriptional mechanisms regulate GXM3 expression and glucuronoxylan methylation.

claims.claim: MSIL2/4 act in addition to the transcriptional network to adjust the final level of GXM enzymes by regulating the translation of the GXM mRNAs.
claims.source: We currently posit that MSIL2/4 act in addition to the transcriptional network to adjust the final level of GXM enzymes by regulating the translation of the GXM mRNAs (Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The model is proposed based on the RNA immunoprecipitation data showing MSIL4 binds GXM mRNAs and the proteomic data showing GXM overaccumulation in msil2/4 mutant, illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The MSIL2/4 mutations are associated with a specific decrease of lignin content in the SCW of the interfascicular fiber cells.
claims.source: Our data indicate that, in addition to the reported change in glucuronoxylan methylation, the MSIL2/4 mutations is also associated with a specific decrease of lignin content in the SCW of the interfascicular fiber cells, whose origin remains unclear.
claims.evidence: The lignin content decrease is measured through acetyl bromide lignin assay and histological staining.

claims.claim: Two lignin biosynthetic enzymes, CAD4 and PAL2, are significantly down-accumulated in msil2/4 mutant.
claims.source: In this regard, although no GO enrichment could be observed for lignin biosynthesis related genes in the proteomic analysis, two lignin biosynthetic enzymes, CAD4 and PAL2, are significantly down-accumulated in msil2/4 mutant (Supplementary file 4)
claims.evidence: The protein down-accumulation is identified in the proteomic analysis shown in Supplementary file 4.

claims.claim: The single cad4 and pal2 knock-out mutants display no significant alteration of lignin content due to genetic redundancy.
claims.source: However, previous published biochemical and genetic analyses do not support this conclusion, as the single cad4 and pal2 knock-out mutants display no significant alteration of lignin content due to genetic redundancy (Sibout et al., 2005; Rohde et al., 2004).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published studies (Sibout et al., 2005; Rohde et al., 2004) showing no lignin phenotype in single cad4 and pal2 mutants.

claims.claim: Thioacidolysis analyses showed that the ratio or degree of polymerization of the different lignin monomers remain unchanged in the msil2/4 mutant.
claims.source: Moreover, thioacidolysis analyses showed that the ratio or degree of polymerization of the different lignin monomers remain unchanged in the msil2/4 mutant
claims.evidence: The lignin composition is analyzed through thioacidolysis showing no significant changes in lignin structure.

claims.claim: The 4-O-methylation of GlcA substituent results in the xylan being more hydrophobic, possibly impacting its interaction with lignin and the capacity of lignin to assemble in the SCW.
claims.source: In this regard, it has been proposed that the 4-O-methylation of GlcA substituent results in the xylan being more hydrophobic, possibly impacting its interaction with lignin and the capacity of lignin to assemble in the SCW (Urbanowicz et al., 2012; Busse-Wicher et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2019; Terrett and Dupree, 2019; Figure 7).
claims.evidence: The hypothesis is supported by citations to published studies (Urbanowicz et al., 2012; Busse-Wicher et al., 2016; Kang et al., 2019; Terrett and Dupree, 2019) proposing the impact of xylan methylation on lignin interaction, illustrated in Figure 7.

claims.claim: A 35S promoter-dependent overexpression study of GXMs in Arabidopsis previously failed to report any discernable developmental or molecular phenotypes associated to a glucuronoxylan hypermethylation.
claims.source: However, a 35 S promoter-dependent overexpression study of GXMs in Arabidopsis previously failed to report any discernable developmental or molecular phenotypes associated to a glucuronoxylan hypermethylation (Yuan et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citation to a published study (Yuan et al., 2014) showing no phenotype in GXM overexpression lines.

results.result: Arabidopsis contains a family of four RNA-binding proteins (MSIL1-4) that are homologous to animal Musashi proteins, featuring conserved RRM domains and widespread expression across land plants.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C4 collectively establish the existence and characteristics of the MSIL protein family through phylogenetic analysis (C1), domain architecture prediction (C2), expression profiling (C3), and evolutionary conservation (C4). The evidence includes sequence alignments, structural modeling, and database searches presented in multiple figures.

results.result: MSIL2 and MSIL4 proteins localize to the cytoplasm in Arabidopsis root cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C5 is supported by fluorescence microscopy data showing GFP-tagged MSIL2 and MSIL4 proteins exhibit diffuse cytoplasmic distribution, contrasting with the nuclear-cytoplasmic distribution of free GFP control (Figure 1D).

results.result: MSIL2 and MSIL4 function redundantly to control multiple aspects of Arabidopsis development, including leaf morphology, senescence, and stem rigidity.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C9 and C50 demonstrate functional redundancy through genetic analysis showing only the msil2/4 double mutant exhibits developmental phenotypes (C6), the quadruple mutant shows no additional defects (C7), and either MSIL2 or MSIL4 can rescue all phenotypes (C8). The complementation experiments provide strong evidence for redundant function.

results.result: MSIL proteins share structural similarity with animal MSI proteins in their RRM domains, adopting the characteristic RRM fold with conserved RNA-binding residues.
results.evaluation: Claims C10-C12 are supported by sequence alignments showing high identity percentages (C10), homology modeling using SWISS-MODEL and AlphaFold2 (C11), and structural predictions showing the characteristic four-stranded β-sheet fold with conserved phenylalanine residues (C12). The structural predictions are consistent with established RRM structure knowledge.

results.result: MSIL2/4 proteins possess RRM-dependent RNA-binding activity that is essential for their in vivo function.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C16 and C54 establish RNA-binding capability through published proteomics data (C13), in vitro binding assays (C14), and functional complementation showing that RRM mutants cannot rescue the msil2/4 phenotype (C15). The convergence of biochemical and genetic evidence strongly supports the requirement for RNA-binding activity.

results.result: MSIL2 and MSIL4 share similar protein interaction networks enriched in mRNA-binding and translational regulatory proteins.
results.evaluation: Claims C17-C18 are supported by affinity purification-MS data showing 27 shared interacting proteins with significant GO enrichment in poly(A) binding, mRNA 3'-UTR binding, and translation initiation factor activity. The proteomic analysis provides direct evidence for the interaction network composition.

results.result: MSIL2/4 proteins localize to stress granules upon heat stress in a translation-dependent manner.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C20 demonstrate stress granule localization through colocalization with PAB2R marker (C19) and sensitivity to cycloheximide treatment (C20). The fluorescence microscopy data and pharmacological validation provide strong evidence for stress granule association.

results.result: MSIL2/4 mutations cause fiber-specific alterations in secondary cell wall formation, including reduced wall thickness, decreased lignin content, altered cellulose accessibility, and reduced biomass recalcitrance.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C29, C55, and C69 collectively demonstrate SCW defects through tissue-specific expression data (C21), quantitative measurements of wall thickness (C22), multiple lignin assays (C23-C25), cellulose staining (C26), and saccharification assays (C27-C28). The fiber-specific effect is supported by the absence of xylem collapse (C55). Multiple independent methods converge on the same conclusion.

results.result: Transcriptomic analysis reveals that MSIL2/4 mutations do not significantly affect expression of SCW biosynthesis genes but upregulate defense-related genes.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C32 are supported by RNA-seq data showing 234 differentially expressed genes (C30), absence of SCW biosynthesis genes from the DEG list (C31), and GO enrichment in defense pathways (C32). The transcriptomic data are consistent with post-transcriptional regulation of SCW genes.

results.result: MSIL2/4 mutations cause overaccumulation of glucuronoxylan biosynthetic enzymes at the protein level without corresponding changes in mRNA levels, indicating translational regulation.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 and C61-C63 demonstrate post-transcriptional regulation through proteomic analysis showing overaccumulation of glucuronoxylan enzymes (C33-C35, C63) without mRNA changes (C36, C61), supporting translational control (C62). The disconnect between mRNA and protein levels provides strong evidence for post-transcriptional regulation.

results.result: MSIL2/4 mutations alter glucuronoxylan decoration patterns without changing total glucuronoxylan or cellulose content.
results.evaluation: Claims C37-C41 are supported by monosaccharide composition analysis showing unchanged glucose and xylose levels (C37-C38), immunofluorescence with LM11 showing unchanged total glucuronoxylan (C39), and LM10 showing decreased signal indicating altered decoration (C40). The combination of biochemical and immunological methods supports the conclusion about decoration changes.

results.result: MSIL2/4 proteins regulate glucuronoxylan 4-O-methylation by binding and repressing translation of GXM1/3 mRNAs, leading to increased methylation in the mutant.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C49 and C66-C68 establish the mechanism through MALDI-TOF analysis showing decreased GlcA and increased meGlcA oligosaccharides (C42-C46), RNA immunoprecipitation showing MSIL4 binds GXM mRNAs (C48), and complementation confirming specificity (C44). The convergence of mass spectrometry, biochemical, and molecular data strongly supports the proposed translational repression mechanism.

results.result: The mechanism underlying reduced lignin content in msil2/4 mutant remains unclear, as lignin biosynthetic enzymes CAD4 and PAL2 are down-accumulated but their single mutants show no lignin phenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 present conflicting evidence: proteomic data show CAD4 and PAL2 down-accumulation (C70), but published studies indicate their single mutants have no lignin phenotype due to redundancy (C71), and thioacidolysis shows unchanged lignin structure (C72). The authors acknowledge the mechanism remains unclear, and the evidence does not support a direct role for MSIL2/4 in lignin biosynthesis regulation.

results.result: MSIL2/4 function is interpreted in the context of animal MSI biology, cell-type-specific regulation, and existing knowledge of SCW biosynthesis and cell wall mutant phenotypes.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C53 and C56-C60 provide contextual interpretation supported by appropriate citations to published literature. Claims C64-C65 and C73-C74 discuss mechanistic interpretations with proper citation support. These claims appropriately place the findings in the broader scientific context, though some represent speculative interpretations (C73) that are clearly identified as such.

results.result: Arabidopsis harbors a family of four RNA-binding proteins (MSIL1-4) that share sequence, domain organization, and structural similarities with animal Musashi proteins. These proteins contain two N-terminal RNA recognition motifs (RRM1 and RRM2) followed by a poorly conserved C-terminal region, are widely expressed in Arabidopsis, and have orthologs distributed across land plants.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept the characterization of the MSIL protein family. Reviewer 3 explicitly notes 'basic characterization of knockout mutations is really well done' and acknowledges the structural and sequence similarities. No reviewer questions the phylogenetic analysis, domain architecture, or expression patterns presented in Figure 1.

results.result: MSIL2 and MSIL4 proteins show diffuse cytoplasmic localization under normal conditions and are recruited to stress granules upon heat stress, as demonstrated by colocalization with PAB2R and sensitivity to cycloheximide treatment.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the subcellular localization data. Reviewer 1 notes that authors 'localized MSIL2 & 4 to stress granules, implicating the RNA-binding function.' Reviewer 3 confirms 'MSL proteins are cytoplasmic' as a central observation. The stress granule localization is not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: The msil2/4 double mutant shows developmental abnormalities including enlarged and curled leaves, early leaf senescence, and pendant inflorescence stem. The quadruple mutant shows no additional phenotypes beyond the double mutant, and ectopic expression of either MSIL2 or MSIL4 rescues all phenotypes, demonstrating functional redundancy.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept the genetic characterization and complementation data. Reviewer 2 states 'The plant phenotypes could be complemented by the wild-type version of either protein' and Reviewer 3 notes 'Knockout of MSL2/4 (but no other double mutant) produces a clear leaf phenotype, and a remarkable stem phenotype.' The functional redundancy is explicitly acknowledged by multiple reviewers.

results.result: MSILs share structural similarity with metazoan MSIs in their RRM domains, which adopt the characteristic RRM fold with conserved phenylalanine residues. MSIL4 exhibits intrinsic RNA-binding activity in vitro, and RRM-dependent RNA-binding is essential for MSIL2/4 function in vivo, as demonstrated by failure of RRM mutants to rescue the msil2/4 phenotype.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the RNA-binding characterization. Reviewer 1 states 'the authors localized MSIL2 & 4 to stress granules, implicating the RNA-binding function of MSIL4 in the cell wall phenotype' and notes 'The phenotypes of knockout mutants persist in point mutants defective in RNA-binding, indicating that RNA-binding is required for biological activity.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'site-directed mutagenesis of MSIL4 conserved RNA-binding motifs, and in vitro RNA binding assays support the conclusion.'

results.result: MSIL2 and MSIL4 exhibit similar protein interaction networks with 27 common interacting proteins, enriched in GO molecular functions related to poly(A) binding, mRNA 3'-UTR binding, single-stranded RNA binding, and translation initiation factor activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the interactome data. Reviewer 2 states 'MSIL2/4 interact with proteins associated with mRNA 3'UTR binding and translational regulation.' Reviewer 3 notes 'associate physically with other RNA-binding proteins and translation factors' as a central observation. The GO enrichment analysis is not questioned.

results.result: MSIL2/4 genes are highly expressed in secondary cell wall-forming interfascicular fiber and xylem vessel cells. The msil2/4 mutant shows significantly thinner secondary cell walls in interfascicular fibers, reduced lignin content (30% decrease), unchanged lignin structure, increased cellulose accessibility, and enhanced saccharification efficiency.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept the secondary cell wall phenotypes. Reviewer 1 states 'the secondary cell wall phenotypes included changes in vasculature morphology, and minor changes to lignin and hemicellulose.' Reviewer 2 notes 'Quantitative analyses of proteins and transcripts in msil2/4 stems uncovered transcriptional upregulation of several xylan-related enzymes' and confirms 'The molecular links between overmethylated xylans and the observed stem defects (which include subtle reductions in lignin and increases beta-glucan polymer distribution).' Reviewer 3 states 'The msl2/4 mutants present multiple defects in secondary cell wall composition and structure, probably explaining their inability to grow upright.'

results.result: RNA-seq analysis identified 234 differentially expressed genes in msil2/4 mutant (156 up-regulated, 78 down-regulated). Notably, genes encoding secondary cell wall biosynthesis enzymes and regulators showed no significant expression changes. GO analysis revealed enrichment in defense and stress response pathways.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the transcriptomic findings. Reviewer 1 explicitly states 'While there were no changes to likely cell wall target genes in the transcriptome of msil2msil4 plants' and notes the defense pathway activation. Reviewer 3 acknowledges 'Msl2/4 mutants show transcriptomic changes with at large two big categories of differentially expressed genes' including defense-related genes. The absence of SCW gene expression changes is a key finding accepted by all reviewers.

results.result: Proteomic analysis revealed 267 differentially abundant proteins in msil2/4 mutant, with strong enrichment of glucuronoxylan biosynthesis enzymes (IRX9/10/14, ESK1, GUX1, GXM3) among up-regulated proteins. These proteomic changes occurred without corresponding mRNA level changes, indicating post-transcriptional regulation.
results.evaluation: All reviewers accept the proteomic evidence for post-transcriptional control. Reviewer 1 states 'proteomics experiments found glucuronoxylan biosynthesis components were upregulated in the mutants' and notes 'despite WT-like RNA levels.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'Quantitative analyses of proteins and transcripts in msil2/4 stems uncovered transcriptional upregulation of several xylan-related enzymes (despite WT-like RNA levels).' Reviewer 3 acknowledges the evidence supports 'post-transcriptional control' though cautions against concluding specifically 'translational control.'

results.result: Monosaccharide composition analysis showed no substantial changes in glucose, xylose, or primary cell wall monosaccharides in msil2/4 mutant. Immunofluorescence with LM11 antibody showed similar glucuronoxylan content, but LM10 antibody revealed decreased signal in interfascicular fibers, indicating altered glucuronoxylan decoration.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the glucuronoxylan decoration changes. Reviewer 1 notes 'they detected an increase in substituted xylan via several methods.' Reviewer 2 states the authors 'propose a model in which MSIL2/4 negatively regulate the translation of GXM (glucuronoxylan methyltransferase).' The immunofluorescence data supporting altered decoration is not questioned by any reviewer.

results.result: MALDI-TOF analysis revealed strongly decreased GlcA-branched xylo-oligomers in msil2/4 mutant, with corresponding increase in methylated GlcA (meGlcA) branched oligomers after normalization. These molecular phenotypes were rescued in complemented lines, indicating MSIL2/4 mutations unleash GXM1/3 activity.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the MALDI-TOF evidence for glucuronoxylan hypermethylation. Reviewer 1 states 'they detected an increase in substituted xylan via several methods' and notes 'Consistent with MALDI-TOF data for released xylan oligosaccharides.' Reviewer 2 confirms 'the authors propose a model in which MSIL2/4 negatively regulate the translation of GXM (glucuronoxylan methyltransferase), a presumed rate-limiting step.' The complementation rescue is accepted as confirming specificity.

results.result: RNA immunoprecipitation assays demonstrated that GXM3 and GXM1 mRNAs are efficiently pulled down by MSIL4 but not by the RRM mutant MSIL4RRM. This indicates MSIL2/4 control glucuronoxylan 4-O-methylation by repressing GXM1/3 mRNA activity through direct RNA binding.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the RNA-IP evidence for direct mRNA targeting. Reviewer 1 states 'Finally, they documented MSIL4 binding to RNA encoding one of these targets, suggesting that MSIL2 and MSIL4 act to post-transcriptionally regulate glucuronoxylan modification.' Reviewer 3 notes 'Two of the mRNAs encoding cell wall factors with significant upregulation in msl2/4 mutants compared to wild type also associate physically with MSL4 as judged by RNA-immunoprecipitation-RT-PCR assays, and this physical association is abrogated in the RNA-binding deficient MSL4 mutant.'

results.result: MSIL2 and MSIL4 function redundantly to promote secondary cell wall formation specifically in interfascicular fibers through RNA-binding-dependent mechanisms. The fiber-specific effect contrasts with constitutive MSIL2/4 expression, suggesting cell-context-dependent activity. MSIL2/4 exert multilevel control on the glucuronoxylan pathway, with GXM-mediated methylation as a rate-limiting step.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the fiber-specific function and multilevel control model. Reviewer 2 notes 'it is intriguing that the loss of the broadly expressed MSIL2/4 genes only significantly affects specific cell types in the stem' and states this 'warrants further investigation in future studies' but does not challenge the finding. Reviewer 1 acknowledges the evidence for 'a new mechanism by which cell wall composition could be regulated.' The rate-limiting step conclusion is supported by the correlation between GXM3 overaccumulation and hypermethylation.

results.result: The msil2/4 mutations are associated with a specific 30% decrease in lignin content in interfascicular fiber cells. Two lignin biosynthetic enzymes (CAD4, PAL2) are down-accumulated, but single mutants show no lignin phenotype due to redundancy. Thioacidolysis showed unchanged lignin structure. The authors propose that increased xylan methylation may impact lignin-xylan interactions and lignin assembly.
results.evaluation: Reviewers express uncertainty about the lignin phenotype mechanism. Reviewer 1 states 'the link between the striking plant phenotype and GXM misregulation is unclear since GXM overexpression doesn't alter plant phenotypes or lignin content (Yuan et al 2014 Plant Science), so misregulation of GXMs in msil2msil4 mutants clearly is not the whole story.' Reviewer 2 notes 'The molecular links between overmethylated xylans and the observed stem defects (which include subtle reductions in lignin and increases beta-glucan polymer distribution) warrants further investigation in future studies.' The lignin decrease is accepted as real, but its mechanistic connection to GXM misregulation remains unclear.

results.result: Differentially expressed genes in msil2/4 mutant are enriched in defense and stress response pathways. The constitutive activation of defense pathways has been well documented in cell wall mutants.
results.evaluation: Reviewer 3 raises significant concerns about alternative interpretation: 'The fact that immune responses are switched on in msl2/4 mutants could also mean that MSL2/4 have biological functions unrelated to cell wall metabolism in wild type plants, and that cell wall defects arise solely as an indirect effect of immune activation.' The reviewer states 'I do not think that the reverse scenario can be formally excluded with the evidence at hand' and requests 'a discussion listing arguments in favor of the direct effect proposed here.' While the reviewer is 'close to being convinced' of the direct effect, the uncertainty about causality remains.

results.result: The pleiotropy of msil2/4 mutation likely results from multifunctionality of these proteins, similar to animal MSI functions. The animal PABP is a functional partner of MSI essential for translation repression. MSILs and RBGDs have diverged in function, as rbgd2/4 shows no developmental phenotypes. Animal MSI2 shows cell-type-specific activities despite ubiquitous expression.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept the comparisons to animal MSI functions and the interpretation of pleiotropy. Reviewer 1 notes the authors 'found that two Musashi-type RNA-binding proteins, MSIL2 and MSIL4 are redundantly required for secondary cell wall development' and accepts the parallel to animal systems. The divergence from RBGDs and cell-type specificity are not questioned by reviewers.

results.result: Previous studies show that transcriptional regulators (NST1, NST3) control cell-lineage-specific SCW formation, and that glucuronoxylan and cellulose levels are correlated in SCW. A prior GXM overexpression study failed to report phenotypes associated with glucuronoxylan hypermethylation.
results.evaluation: These literature-based claims are accepted by reviewers. Reviewer 1 explicitly cites the Yuan et al. 2014 study showing 'GXM overexpression doesn't alter plant phenotypes or lignin content' as a point of comparison. The transcriptional control by NST1/NST3 is accepted background knowledge not questioned by any reviewer.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on MSIL protein family characterization (C1-C4). Both evaluations find the phylogenetic analysis, domain architecture, expression profiling, and evolutionary conservation well-supported. Peer reviewers explicitly note the 'basic characterization of knockout mutations is really well done.'

Both support subcellular localization claims, but peer review R2 addresses broader localization context (C5, C19, C20) including stress granule association, while OpenEval R2 focuses only on cytoplasmic distribution (C5). OpenEval addresses stress granule localization separately in R7.

Both support stress granule localization (C19, C20). OpenEval R7 emphasizes colocalization with PAB2R and cycloheximide sensitivity, while peer review R2 groups this with general subcellular localization findings. Complete agreement on the evidence quality.

Perfect agreement on functional redundancy (C6-C9, C50). Both evaluations accept the genetic evidence showing only msil2/4 double mutant exhibits phenotypes, quadruple mutant shows no additional defects, and complementation demonstrates redundant function. Peer reviewers describe the stem phenotype as 'remarkable.'

Both support RRM structural predictions (C10-C12), but peer review R4 addresses broader RNA-binding characterization including functional evidence (C13-C16) that OpenEval addresses separately in R5. Agreement on structural modeling quality.

Both support RNA-binding capability (C13-C16), with OpenEval R5 emphasizing convergence of proteomics, in vitro assays, and genetic complementation. Peer review R4 groups structural and functional RNA-binding evidence together. Complete agreement that RNA-binding is required for biological activity.

Perfect agreement on interactome data (C17-C18). Both evaluations accept the affinity purification-MS showing 27 shared interacting proteins and GO enrichment in poly(A) binding, mRNA 3'-UTR binding, and translation factors. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Strong agreement on secondary cell wall defects (C21-C29). OpenEval R8 includes additional claims about fiber-specific effects (C55, C69) not explicitly addressed in peer review R6. Both accept multiple independent methods showing wall thickness, lignin, cellulose, and saccharification changes. Peer reviewers note 'multiple defects in secondary cell wall composition and structure.'

Perfect agreement on transcriptomic findings (C30-C32). Both evaluations accept that RNA-seq shows 234 DEGs, absence of SCW biosynthesis genes from DEG list, and GO enrichment in defense pathways. This absence of transcriptional changes is recognized as key evidence for post-transcriptional regulation.

Perfect agreement on post-transcriptional regulation evidence (C33-C36, C61-C63). Both evaluations accept proteomic data showing glucuronoxylan enzyme overaccumulation without mRNA changes. Peer review R8 notes this supports 'post-transcriptional control' but cautions against concluding specifically 'translational control' without additional evidence.

Perfect agreement on glucuronoxylan decoration changes (C37-C41). Both evaluations accept monosaccharide composition analysis, immunofluorescence with LM11 and LM10 antibodies showing unchanged total glucuronoxylan but altered decoration. No concerns raised by either evaluation.

Both support MALDI-TOF evidence for glucuronoxylan hypermethylation (C42-C47). OpenEval R12 addresses broader mechanistic claims including RNA-IP and complementation (C48-C49, C66-C68), while peer review R10 focuses on the methylation changes and GXM translational repression model. Agreement on core biochemical findings.

Both support RNA-IP evidence for direct mRNA targeting (C48-C49, C68). OpenEval R12 groups this with broader mechanistic evidence, while peer review R11 focuses specifically on the RNA-IP data showing MSIL4 binding to GXM mRNAs and loss of binding in RNA-binding deficient mutants. Complete agreement on evidence quality.

Perfect agreement on uncertainty regarding lignin phenotype mechanism (C70-C72). Both evaluations note conflicting evidence: proteomic data show CAD4/PAL2 down-accumulation, but single mutants have no lignin phenotype due to redundancy, and thioacidolysis shows unchanged lignin structure. Both acknowledge the mechanism remains unclear and is not fully explained by GXM misregulation.

Divergent evaluations of defense pathway activation (C32). OpenEval R9 supports this as straightforward transcriptomic finding, while peer review R14 raises uncertainty about whether defense activation is secondary to cell wall defects or indicates an alternative primary function of MSIL2/4 unrelated to cell wall metabolism. Peer reviewer requests discussion of causality.

Both support contextual claims about MSI function comparisons and pleiotropy (C51-C53, C59). OpenEval R14 addresses broader set of literature-based claims (C56-C60, C64-C65, C73-C74), while peer review R15 focuses on animal MSI parallels and cell-type specificity. Agreement on appropriateness of comparative interpretations.

Both support literature-based contextual claims (C56, C65, C74). OpenEval R14 groups these with other interpretive claims, while peer review R16 specifically validates citations to Yuan et al. 2014 and transcriptional control by NST1/NST3. Agreement that background literature is appropriately cited.

Both support fiber-specific function and multilevel control interpretations (C57-C58, C64). OpenEval R14 treats these as contextual interpretations, while peer review R12 notes the fiber-specificity 'warrants further investigation' but accepts the finding. Agreement on evidence, with peer review noting need for future mechanistic studies.

Divergent evaluations of alternative interpretation (C60). OpenEval R14 supports this as appropriate contextual discussion, while peer review R14 expresses significant uncertainty about whether cell wall defects are direct or indirect effects of immune activation. Peer reviewer requests explicit discussion of arguments favoring direct effect.

Minor overlap on RNA-binding requirement claim (C54). OpenEval R5 includes this with broader RNA-binding evidence, while peer review R12 addresses it in context of fiber-specific function. Both support the claim but in different analytical contexts.

Minor overlap on fiber-specific SCW defects (C69). OpenEval R8 supports this as part of comprehensive SCW phenotype characterization, while peer review R13 addresses it in context of uncertain lignin mechanism. Agreement on the observation, but different analytical groupings.

Minor overlap on fiber-specific effect (C55). OpenEval R8 includes absence of xylem collapse as supporting fiber-specificity, while peer review R12 notes this finding warrants further investigation. Agreement on observation, slight difference in emphasis on mechanistic implications.

Minor overlap on mechanistic speculation (C73). OpenEval R14 supports this as appropriately identified speculation, while peer review R13 expresses uncertainty about the link between GXM misregulation and lignin phenotype. Both recognize limitations in current mechanistic understanding.

Minor overlap on rate-limiting step and correlation claims (C66-C67). OpenEval R12 supports these as part of comprehensive mechanistic evidence, while peer review R12 accepts the model but notes molecular links to stem defects warrant further investigation. Agreement on evidence, with peer review emphasizing need for additional mechanistic studies.
